title: With Due Respect (Vol. 4) -- Ch. 8: Restore Amla's Fangs
primary_topics: Chapter 8 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 4) -- CJP's July 11, 2010 Inquirer column arguing that the Supreme Court 'partially defanged' the Anti-Money Laundering Act (Amla) by requiring courts to notify depositors before issuing bank inquiry orders -- 'equivalent to telling a thief to hide his loot'

How Amla works (RA 9160 of 2001, amended by RA 9194 of 2003) -- defining money laundering and providing two provisional remedies, 'freeze orders' and 'bank inquiry orders,' the latter used by the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) to trace alleged bribes after Agan v. Piatco nullified the NAIA Terminal 3 deal

The ruling in Republic v. Eugenio (Feb. 14, 2008), which allowed ex parte bank inquiries for a short list of crimes but not for graft, and held that courts must first notify account holders and hold a hearing -- and, citing the Bank Secrecy Act (RA 1405), barred inquiries into a couple's joint conjugal account

CJP's call for the Aquino administration to 'restore the fangs of Amla' -- by petitioning the Court (in a proper case) to allow ex parte inquiries or at least reverse the joint-account exemption, and by asking Congress to amend Amla to authorize ex parte inquiries and modify the bank-secrecy policy as to ill-gotten wealth
sub_topics: The thesis: 'one sure way of catching big-time grafters is by tracing their loot' and freezing 'ill-gotten bank deposits,' but the Court 'partially' defanged Amla by requiring courts to 'notify the depositors' before issuing bank inquiry orders -- which CJP likens to 'telling a thief to hide his loot lest the police discover and seize it'

Background: enacted in 2001 as RA 9160 and amended in 2003 by RA 9194, Amla defines money laundering as transacting the proceeds of an unlawful activity to 'make them appear to have originated from legitimate sources' -- a crime 'punished in many countries' (a Paris court had just convicted ex-dictator Manuel Noriega for laundering drug kickbacks through French banks)

The tools and the trigger: Amla provides 'freeze orders' and 'bank inquiry orders'; after Agan v. Piatco (May 5, 2003) nullified the Piatco concession for NAIA Terminal 3, the AMLC used bank inquiries -- and lower courts granted its ex parte application to examine the accounts of four individuals, including a former Cabinet member

The challenge: one of the four, and the wife of another (over a joint conjugal account), argued that courts must give 'prior notice' and an opportunity to oppose, the wife contending that ex parte grants violated her constitutional rights to privacy and due process

Republic v. Eugenio (Feb. 14, 2008): the Court (Second Division, per Justice Dante Tinga) conceded that Section 11 allows ex parte inquiry for accounts tied to kidnapping for ransom, dangerous drugs, hijacking, destructive arson and murder -- but not for 'other criminal activities including graft,' since Section 11 (unlike Section 10's explicit 20-day freeze orders) 'omits any reference to ex parte applications'

The notice-and-hearing rule: the Court held that courts must first notify account holders and hold a hearing, conceding inquiries would be 'harder to obtain' but reasoning that bank records would stay intact -- a rationale CJP rejects, since 'the depositor, once alerted, will... surely empty the account too'

The privacy overlay: the Court tied Section 11 to the right to privacy under the Bank Secrecy Act (RA 1405 of 1955), stressed that 'the absolute confidentiality of bank deposits remains a basic state policy,' and barred inquiries into the couple's joint conjugal account -- so, CJP notes wryly, 'to frustrate bank inquiry orders, one needs only to utilize a joint account. Hmmm'

The reform call: to make its anti-corruption campaign succeed, the Aquino administration must 'restore the fangs of Amla' -- first by petitioning the Court to allow ex parte inquiries or at least reverse the joint-conjugal-account exemption, and second by asking Congress to amend Amla to authorize ex parte inquiries (as it did freeze orders) and to modify the bank-secrecy policy 'vis-a-vis ill-gotten wealth'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 8 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 4), CJP's July 11, 2010 Inquirer column, argues that the Supreme Court 'partially defanged' the Anti-Money Laundering Act (Amla) by requiring courts to notify depositors before issuing bank inquiry orders -- a rule he likens to 'telling a thief to hide his loot lest the police discover and seize it.' Enacted as RA 9160 (2001) and amended by RA 9194 (2003), Amla defines money laundering as transacting unlawful proceeds to make them 'appear to have originated from legitimate sources' (a crime, he notes, for which a Paris court had just convicted ex-dictator Manuel Noriega), and provides two tools: 'freeze orders' and 'bank inquiry orders.' After Agan v. Piatco voided the NAIA Terminal 3 concession, the Anti-Money Laundering Council used bank inquiries -- winning lower-court ex parte access to four people's accounts, including a former Cabinet member's -- until one holder and a wife (over a joint conjugal account) challenged the orders as violating privacy and due process. In Republic v. Eugenio (2008, per Justice Tinga), the Court allowed ex parte inquiries for kidnapping, drugs, hijacking, arson and murder, but not for graft -- since Section 11, unlike Section 10's explicit 20-day freeze orders, 'omits any reference to ex parte applications' -- and required prior notice and a hearing, reasoning the bank records would remain intact. CJP rejects that reasoning: 'the depositor, once alerted, will... surely empty the account too.' Worse, the Court leaned on the Bank Secrecy Act (RA 1405) to hold that 'the absolute confidentiality of bank deposits remains a basic state policy' and to exempt the joint conjugal account -- so, he notes wryly, 'to frustrate bank inquiry orders, one needs only to utilize a joint account. Hmmm.' To make its anti-corruption campaign succeed, he concludes, the Aquino administration must 'restore the fangs of Amla' -- petitioning the Court to allow ex parte inquiries or at least reverse the joint-account exemption, and asking Congress to amend Amla to authorize ex parte inquiries and to modify the bank-secrecy policy as to ill-gotten wealth.
